text: Joiner/mover/leaver automation will miss things - Lesson 21 showed exactly how. Access certification campaigns are the structured check built on top of that assumption: a periodic review where the people who actually understand a user's job have to look at their access list and vouch for it, line by line.

A certification campaign presents a manager or a resource owner with exactly who currently has access to what, and asks for one of two decisions on each line: keep it, or revoke it. This has to be a human with real context, because IT can see that someone has access - only their manager or the system owner can credibly say whether they still need it.

Most organizations run these campaigns quarterly for sensitive, audit-relevant systems like financial ERP modules, and semi-annually or annually for lower-risk systems - not continuously, because a scheduled campaign with a deadline gets real attention in a way a constant trickle of micro-reviews doesn't. The core mechanic is attestation: the reviewer must explicitly mark each grant as still needed. Anything not explicitly attested to by the deadline is revoked automatically - silence counts as a no, not a yes, which is exactly what stops reviewers from just clicking approve on everything.

Here's what that catches in practice. David moved from AP to Procurement, but still holds vendor payment approval access from his time on AP. His current manager has no reason to notice this on her own - but the campaign puts the burden on her to decide on every single line, not just the ones that stand out. She can't confidently say he still needs it, so she flags it, and it's revoked within days.

Without the campaign, that leftover access could have sat unnoticed for years - a textbook case of the mover-driven access creep from Lesson 21. It's also, as we'll see next, exactly the kind of access combination that becomes genuinely dangerous if David retains procurement-side permissions too. That's separation of duties and toxic combinations, coming up in Lesson 23.
